result:
The first thing Daniel fixed after retiring was a drawer that had been stuck for eleven years.

He had developed a way of opening it: lift the left corner, brace one knee against the cabinet, then pull with an irritation so practiced it no longer felt like irritation. Inside were batteries, takeaway menus, and keys whose locks had disappeared.

The repair took nine minutes. A screwdriver, a little sanding, a rub of candle wax along the runner.

Afterward, he opened and closed the drawer several times.

His wife came into the kitchen.

“Look,” he said.

She looked.

“The drawer.”

“I see.”

“It works.”

She opened it herself, then shut it. “Well,” she said, and put the kettle on.

For a moment he was disappointed. He had expected something more, though he couldn’t have said what.

That afternoon he repaired the loose latch on the garden gate. The next day, he glued a chair rung and left the chair upside down on the table, where it looked like a large, defeated beetle.

By Friday he had made a list.

His wife found him in the hallway, studying a patch of peeling wallpaper.

“Before you start,” she said, “come out with me.”

“Where?”

“Nowhere special.”

They walked to the shops by the longer route. Outside the school, someone had dropped a blue mitten. His wife picked it up and fitted it over a railing spike, where it stood with its small thumb extended.

On the way home they bought bread they didn’t need.

At lunch, Daniel reached for the drawer. His knee rose automatically to brace the cabinet, and he laughed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

He put the bread knife away. The drawer slid shut under one finger.

Later, he added the wallpaper to his list. Then he folded the paper and slipped it beneath a salt cellar.

They had half a loaf left. He cut two thick slices for toast, and when his wife asked whether he wanted to take them into the garden, he said yes.
